vocabulary.name: States of water
vocabulary.description: Solid, liquid and gas; melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation, boiling.

vocabulary.name: The water cycle
vocabulary.description: Evaporation → clouds → precipitation → collection; the Sun as the driver; the cycle as a system.

vocabulary.name: Rain and the monsoon
vocabulary.description: Rainfall, monsoon winds, seasons and climate patterns, humidity, weather measurement.

vocabulary.name: Rivers and landforms
vocabulary.description: Rivers from source to sea, erosion and deposition, valleys, deltas, floods, glaciers.

vocabulary.name: Oceans and water bodies
vocabulary.description: Oceans, seas, lakes, ponds; how water is distributed on Earth; tides and currents.

vocabulary.name: Water as a resource
vocabulary.description: Sources, scarcity, conservation, rainwater harvesting, wells, tanks, dams, irrigation, supply.

vocabulary.name: Water and life
vocabulary.description: Water in the body, in plants, aquatic habitats, drinking water, health and sanitation.

vocabulary.name: Water as a solvent
vocabulary.description: Dissolving, solutions, mixtures, purification and separation.

vocabulary.name: Measuring water
vocabulary.description: Capacity and volume in litres, weighing liquids, measuring water temperature.

vocabulary.name: Water and heat
vocabulary.description: Heating and cooling water, convection, sea and land breezes, water in heat transfer.

vocabulary.name: Water in society
vocabulary.description: Civilisations by rivers, water in architecture, urban supply, community disputes, water in stories.

chapters.title: Madhu's Wish
chapters.one_line: A boy who shares his lunch is granted a wish by a magical banyan tree, asks for endless food and no water, and learns through unstoppable hiccups that water matters more than any feast.

concepts.statement: In Sudha Murty's story a magical tree grants Madhu every kind of food but no water, and the tale's whole moral is that water is worth more than any feast.
concepts.section_ref: Section A: Madhu's Wish (prose_summary) / Let us think B.3 'Do you think water is important? Why do you think so?'

concepts.statement: When hiccups strike, sharbat, kheer and badam milk cannot stop them and only a jug of water can, so children talk about why the body needs water above all other food.
concepts.section_ref: Let us listen A.2 (transcript) / Let us think B.1–3 / Let us write A.4 'Madhu asked for water because ___'

chapters.subject: english

chapters.title: Filling and Lifting
chapters.one_line: Introduces capacity by comparing and pouring between vessels, names the litre (with half and quarter litre) as its standard unit, then introduces weight comparison, the kilogram and pan-balance reasoning.

concepts.statement: How much a vessel holds cannot be judged by its shape, so water or milk is poured into same-sized glasses to compare fairly, and the litre (then half and quarter litre) is met as the standard unit by checking a bucket, mug and glass against a 1-litre bottle.
concepts.section_ref: S1 Whose glass holds more? (T-4, T-5) / S2 A Measuring Bottle — the litre (T-13, T-14, T-16)

chapters.subject: mathematics

chapters.title: Water–A Precious Gift
chapters.one_line: Children observe rain, follow where rainwater goes, trace where their household water comes from and how it is stored, and learn that every drop must be saved.

concepts.statement: Rain is met by direct observation: children read sky and nature clues to predict whether it will rain, then watch a shower and describe its heaviness, drop size, speed and slant, and collect rainwater to see whether it looks clean or dirty.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Here Comes the Rain! / T-1, T-2, T-3

concepts.statement: After rain falls it soaks into the soil, runs into streams and rivers, collects in puddles, ponds and lakes, or is stored underground as groundwater that feeds wells — the cycle grounded at a concrete, observable level without the formal 'water cycle' term.
concepts.section_ref: Section: What happened to the rainwater? / T-4, T-5, T-19

concepts.statement: Streams, rivers, ponds and lakes are the local water bodies where rainwater collects, and students find one near their village or city, visit and draw it, and record whether its water is (or was) used for drinking.
concepts.section_ref: Section: What happened to the rainwater? / T-8; Let us reflect / T-20

concepts.statement: Tap water comes from rooftop tanks, pipes, wells, borewells or tankers; many people must carry water from a distant well, river or lake; households store water against irregular supply; and water is precious, so it must not be wasted or polluted.
concepts.section_ref: Sections: Water is a Precious Gift! / Water in Our Daily Lives / Every Drop Counts (T-10 to T-15, T-22)

concepts.statement: People have long stored water in clay, copper, brass and other traditional vessels, kept pots of water outside their homes for passers-by in the hot months, and celebrate rain and rivers in songs and poems.
concepts.section_ref: Sections: Water is a Precious Gift! / Water in Our Daily Lives / Every Drop Counts (T-6, T-9, T-14, T-17)

concepts.statement: Water is essential for the survival of people, birds and animals, so students build and maintain a birdbath, note which birds and insects come to drink, and ask whether the water near them is fit for drinking.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Every Drop Counts / T-18, T-21; Let us reflect / T-20

concepts.statement: Students estimate how much water everyday tasks need in informal units (mugs of water to brush teeth, water used for a shower) to build a sense of quantity — placed under the nearest id, since no standard units such as litres are used.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Water in Our Daily Lives / T-16

chapters.subject: the_world_around_us

chapters.title: Weigh It, Pour It
chapters.one_line: Revisits weight and capacity from Grade 3, introduces grams and millilitres as sub-units with their fraction relationships to the kilogram and litre, and closes with measuring everyday water use and waste.

concepts.statement: The litre is subdivided into millilitres — 500 ml is half a litre, 250 ml a quarter, 100 ml a tenth — discovered by pouring, with 10 ml dosing cups and 1 ml droppers for tiny amounts, and household containers (water bottle, glass, mug, jug, bucket) are estimated then measured.
concepts.section_ref: S5 Measuring capacity — litre, millilitre, and fractions (T-21, T-22, T-23, T-24, T-27)

concepts.statement: Students count the litres of water they drink and use each day for showering, washing clothes and watering crops, and collect the drip from a leaking tap for an hour to work out how much water is wasted in a day and a week.
concepts.section_ref: S6 Water use, conservation, and measuring containers (T-29, T-30, T-31 Water Conservation in Everyday Life)

explicit_links: The chapter opens by revisiting weight and capacity from Grade 3
chapters.subject: mathematics

chapters.title: Different Lands, Different Lives
chapters.one_line: Four children's holidays introduce India's plains, desert, coast and mountains and how each landform shapes food, clothing, houses, livelihoods and festivals.

concepts.statement: Rainfall differs across landforms and shapes how people live: deserts get very little rain, Sikkim's heavy rain calls for wooden houses with slanting roofs, the rainy season brings landslides in the mountains, and coastal Odisha faces cyclones.
concepts.section_ref: Sections: In the Land of Endless Sand / In the Mountains, with Nayan / On the Seashore, with Chandni (T-12, T-19, T-21)

concepts.statement: Water is scarce in the desert, so plants like cactus, khejri and babool survive by storing water and desert houses keep tankas (water tanks) for storage; students discuss why deserts are short of water.
concepts.section_ref: Section: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika / T-6

concepts.statement: The sea defines the coastal landform: Odisha's coast has beaches, fishing as the main livelihood, sand art and conch shells, and students compare life by the sea with life in the desert and discuss why beaches must be kept clean.
concepts.section_ref: Section: On the Seashore, with Chandni / T-7, T-9, T-10

concepts.statement: The sea along the Odisha coast is a habitat for sea turtles, crabs, dolphins, corals, seaweed and starfish, which students identify by name from pictures.
concepts.section_ref: Section: On the Seashore, with Chandni / T-11

chapters.subject: the_world_around_us

chapters.title: The Frog
chapters.one_line: A first-person poem in which a frog describes its cheerful amphibious life in ponds, drains and grass, from tadpole to webbed-footed hopper.

concepts.statement: A frog lives in water and on land alike — sitting in ponds and muddy drains, swimming first as a tadpole and later with webbed feet — and children compare this amphibious life with a fish's and draw the frog's pond home.
concepts.section_ref: Section A: The Frog (poem_text, poem_appreciation_summary) / Let us Think A.1, A.3, B.1, B.3 / Let us Listen: My Frog's World

chapters.subject: english

chapters.title: What a Tank!
chapters.one_line: An informational text on India's traditional and modern water-storage structures, centred on rural Punjab's rooftop tanks sculpted into flowers, tractors and aeroplanes, with discussion and listening tasks on water wastage and conservation.

concepts.statement: Water has been stored for centuries in structures like Tamil Nadu's ooranis for rainwater harvesting, Kerala's year-round Panam Keni wells and Rajasthan's underground tankas, and today in household overhead tanks — and children list how water is wasted daily, how to stop it, and hear how a day without supply led a family to set up rainwater harvesting at home.
concepts.section_ref: Section A: What a Tank! (prose_summary) / Let us Think A.1, B.1 / Let us Speak A–B / Let us Listen: A Day without Water / Let us Explore A (cleaning tanks)

concepts.statement: Rural Punjab's rooftop water tanks are sculpted from cement and steel into flowers, footballs, roosters, tractors and aeroplanes that announce the owner's occupation or passion, and children design a community poster to preserve and clean old water tanks.
concepts.section_ref: Section A: What a Tank! (prose_summary) / Let us Think A.3–4, B.2 / Let us Write A (poster) / Let us Explore B (The Thirsty Crow)

explicit_links: Find at least five exclamatory sentences from your Grade 4 English textbook
chapters.subject: english

chapters.title: The Decision of the Panchayat
chapters.one_line: A cunning neighbour sells a farmer a well but refuses him its water, and the village Panchayat outwits him with a judgment that the water in another's well belongs to the well's owner.

concepts.statement: A village Panchayat under the banyan tree settles a dispute in which a neighbour who sold a well claims he did not sell the water in it, ruling that water kept in another's well belongs to the well's owner, and children judge whether the decision was fair.
concepts.section_ref: Section A: The Decision of the Panchayat (prose_summary) / Let us Think A.1–4, B.1, B.3

concepts.statement: A farmer buys the well beside his new field because the well is the field's source of water, and the chapter states outright that water is priceless — so valuable that no price can be put on it.
concepts.section_ref: Section A (prose_summary) / Let us Write B 'Water is priceless'

chapters.subject: english

chapters.title: Far and Near
chapters.one_line: Builds the length unit hierarchy from millimetre to kilometre and performs conversions and the four operations on compound lengths.
chapters.skip_reason: Length and distance only; water stations in a race, a well's depth and a waterfall's distance appear as incidental context, never as measured or discussed water.
chapters.subject: mathematics

chapters.title: Weight and Capacity
chapters.one_line: Formalises weight units from milligram to tonne and capacity in litres and millilitres, with double-number-line conversion, comparison and all four operations on compound quantities.

concepts.statement: Litres and millilitres are tied by 1,000 ml = 1 l on a double number line, so 1 l 400 ml is 1,400 ml (not 1,040 ml), and amounts of water, milk, fuel and oil in compound l-and-ml form are compared, added, subtracted, multiplied and divided with regrouping across the 1,000.
concepts.section_ref: S10 Measuring Capacity (T-28, T-29) / S11 Big to Small, Small to Big (T-30, T-31) / S12 l and ml Double Number Line (T-33, T-34, T-35) / S13–S14 (T-36–T-43)

chapters.subject: mathematics

chapters.title: Water — The Essence of Life
chapters.one_line: Freshwater is a tiny share of Earth's water; the chapter builds the three forms of water, the water cycle, groundwater, river flow and freshwater habitats through models and a field visit.

concepts.statement: Most of Earth's surface is covered by water but nearly all of it is salty ocean water unfit for drinking or farming; freshwater is only a tiny fraction (a teaspoon in a glass) held in rivers, ponds, lakes and underground, and India's rivers drain either to the Bay of Bengal or the Arabian Sea.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Water on Earth / T-1, T-2, T-3; Surface Water / T-10; Let us reflect / T-16

concepts.statement: Water exists as liquid (rain), solid (ice) and vapour (steam); students watch droplets condense on a cold steel glass of ice, ice melt, water boil and water left in sunlight for three days disappear, recording that water changes form and can return to liquid.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Water has Different Forms / T-4; Let us reflect / T-15

concepts.statement: The Sun's heat evaporates water from oceans and rivers, the vapour cools into clouds, and rain, snow and hail fall back into rivers, lakes and oceans in a continuous cycle, modelled with coloured water sealed in a transparent bag left in sunlight.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Water Cycle / T-5

concepts.statement: Rainwater percolates through soil and rock to become groundwater drawn up by wells, borewells, tube wells and handpumps; paved city surfaces block recharge while open ground, soak pits, ponds and trees restore it, and students design a house or school that conserves water.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Groundwater / T-6, T-7; Let us reflect / T-18, T-19, T-20

concepts.statement: Rivers begin in mountains and flow downhill with their path and speed shaped by the land they cross (and flowing water reshapes land over time), modelled with mustard seeds on crumpled paper and traced on a map of India's rivers, including the Luni that ends in the Rann of Kutch without reaching a sea.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Surface Water / T-8, T-9, T-10

concepts.statement: All living beings depend on freshwater, and freshwater habitats hold specially adapted plants and animals (fins and gills, waxy leaves; dragonfly, pond heron, freshwater turtle, lotus, water hyacinth) linked in a food chain, which students observe on a visit to a pond, lake or aquarium.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Life in Water / T-11, T-12, T-13, T-14; Let us reflect / T-17

concepts.statement: Communities have built traditional rainwater-harvesting structures such as the johads of Rajasthan (small dams that collect rain and recharge groundwater), and Hiware Bazar in Maharashtra became water-positive through community-led watershed management.
concepts.section_ref: Sections: Water on Earth; Surface Water

explicit_links: This section revisits the three states of water — liquid (rain), solid (ice), and vapour (steam)
chapters.subject: the_world_around_us

chapters.title: Journey of a River
chapters.one_line: The Godavari narrates its own journey from source to delta, showing how a river supports life, is dammed, polluted, floods and runs dry, and what people owe it in return.

concepts.statement: One river is followed source to sea: the Godavari rises as a stream at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats, gathers tributaries over 1,465 km, flows year-round (perennial, unlike seasonal rivers), spreads into a delta where freshwater meets the sea at the Coringa mangroves, and overflows its banks in floods when rain is excessive — worse where forests have been cut.
concepts.section_ref: Sections: Where I Begin, Where I Flow / The Life I Hold / When a River Floods (T-1, T-16)

concepts.statement: A river supplies water for drinking, cooking, washing, irrigation and industry through pipes and canals; India's 900-plus dams store river water for dry seasons, irrigation and electricity at the cost of flooding land and displacing people; and drought (Chennai 2019) forces migration and calls for conservation habits, the National Water Mission and water ATMs.
concepts.section_ref: Sections: The Many Ways I Support Lives / Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow / When a River Runs Dry! (T-3, T-6, T-8, T-18, T-19)

concepts.statement: Some pollutants dissolve invisibly in water while others such as oil do not (a spoon of sugar versus a spoon of cooking oil stirred into two glasses), both harming the river, and students design a simple water filter from everyday materials.
concepts.section_ref: Section: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters / T-13; Let us reflect / T-26

concepts.statement: Waste, plastic, untreated sewage and fertiliser runoff make river water unsafe for people and wildlife — algal 'green blankets' choke aquatic life and make water undrinkable — and floods spread disease and cut off safe drinking water.
concepts.section_ref: Section: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters / T-12, T-14, T-15; When a River Floods / T-16

concepts.statement: Since ancient times settlements have grown beside rivers for reliable water; the Godavari is sacred (Dakshina Ganga, the Pushkaram festival at Nashik), families carry river stories and festivals, and students role-play as Sarpanch or plan a riverside city that stays clean, flood-safe and supplied through summer.
concepts.section_ref: Sections: Where I Begin, Where I Flow / The Many Ways I Support Lives / Let us reflect (T-2, T-17, T-21, T-23, T-27)

concepts.statement: Rainfall governs a river's year: seasonal rivers flow only in the rainy season, excessive rain makes rivers overflow their banks, and dams hold water back for the dry season.
concepts.section_ref: Sections: The Life I Hold / Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow / When a River Floods

chapters.subject: the_world_around_us

chapters.title: Our School—A Happy Place
chapters.one_line: Students explore their own school as 'green school' teams — waste, water, cooling, greenery, traffic and fire safety — and how everyday behaviour makes it a happy place.

concepts.statement: A dripping tap wastes far more water than it seems — students time how long a drip takes to fill a glass and scale it up to a day — and a green school fixes leaks, prevents wastage and collects rainwater, in the spirit of the Jal Shakti Abhiyan.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Dripping Water / T-15, T-16, T-17; Be a School Explorer! (Water Watchers)

concepts.statement: Water is measured two ways: the time a drip takes to fill a glass (scaled to glasses per day), and water temperature read with a thermometer before and after an hour under a tree versus in the Sun.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Dripping Water / T-15; Greenery Around Us / T-20

concepts.statement: Water kept in the shade of a tree stays cooler than water left in the Sun, and clay matkas cool drinking water without electricity by evaporative cooling.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Greenery Around Us / T-20; Dripping Water (IKS note on matkas)

chapters.subject: the_world_around_us

chapters.title: Energy—How Things Work
chapters.one_line: Energy is what makes things move, light up, sound and warm; the chapter covers its sources (food, fuels, electricity) and clean generation from the Sun, wind and flowing water.

concepts.statement: Flowing water is a clean energy source: fast-moving rivers generate electricity and traditional gharaats (watermills) in hilly areas grind grain, modelled with a paper-cup water wheel that turns when water is poured on it — placed under the nearest id, since hydropower is not in the vocabulary.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Generating Energy from the Sun, Wind and Water / T-8, T-12

chapters.subject: the_world_around_us

chapters.title: The Winner (Sports and Wellness)
chapters.one_line: Georgia Heard's short poem about children playing ball in a neighbour's field until night falls and 'wins', taught for typographic pattern and personification.
chapters.skip_reason: Water is only the setting ('next to the creek'); the sole water task is a vocabulary word web naming other water bodies (Let us learn), plus a swimming riddle in Let us listen — incidental, neither taught nor substantively used.
chapters.subject: english

chapters.title: Materials Around Us
chapters.one_line: Objects are made of materials that can be grouped by observable properties — lustre, hardness, transparency, solubility in water, mass and volume — leading to the definition of matter as anything that occupies space and has mass.

concepts.statement: Stirring sugar, salt, chalk powder, sand and sawdust into water shows that some materials dissolve completely (soluble) while others do not (insoluble), some liquids mix with water while others form a separate layer, and gases such as oxygen dissolve too, which is what makes aquatic life possible.
concepts.section_ref: 6.3.4 What is soluble in water; what is not? / Activity 6.7

concepts.statement: The amount of water in a tumbler is its volume — the space it occupies — and bottles labelled 1 L, 500 mL or 200 mL state that volume in litres and millilitres (with 1 m³ = 1000 L noted as the SI relation).
concepts.section_ref: 6.3.6 Space and volume / 6.4 What is Matter?

explicit_links: the distinction between the two will be explored in higher classes
connecting classification of the non-living world to prior learning about classification of the living world
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Temperature and its Measurement
chapters.one_line: Touch is an unreliable judge of hot and cold, so temperature is measured with clinical, laboratory and room thermometers on the Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales.

concepts.statement: A laboratory thermometer is dipped into warm water and read while still immersed, held vertically with the eye level to the liquid column, to measure the water's temperature in degrees Celsius.
concepts.section_ref: 7.3.2 Laboratory thermometer / Activity 7.5

concepts.statement: Boiling water and melting ice each hold a constant temperature, and students' readings of boiling water in Shillong come out slightly below 100 °C, raising the idea that the boiling point of water depends on altitude.
concepts.section_ref: 7.3.2 Laboratory thermometer / Activity 7.6 and 'More to do!'

concepts.statement: Air temperature is a weather measurement: weather services record each day's maximum and minimum air temperature, which rises towards summer and falls in winter and is used in forecasting (this node is weather measurement only, with no water content — recorded because the vocabulary lists weather measurement here).
concepts.section_ref: 7.3.3 Air temperature / Activity 7.7

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: A Journey through States of Water
chapters.one_line: Water exists as ice, liquid water and invisible water vapour; heating and cooling move it between these states, and evaporation and condensation at planetary scale give clouds and rain.

concepts.statement: Water exists as ice, liquid water and water vapour; evaporation (which goes on even at room temperature) and condensation, melting and freezing move it between these states, and evaporation is faster with more exposed surface, higher temperature, moving air and drier air.
concepts.section_ref: 8.1 Investigating Water's Disappearing Act / 8.2 Another Mystery / 8.3 / 8.4 / 8.5 (Activities 8.2, 8.4, 8.5, 8.6, 8.7, 8.8)

concepts.statement: Water vapour rising from oceans, lakes and rivers cools and condenses around dust particles to form clouds, the droplets merge into drops heavy enough to fall as rain (or hail or snow), and the water collects again in oceans, lakes, rivers and groundwater — the water cycle.
concepts.section_ref: 8.7 How Do Clouds Give Us Rain? / Activities 8.10, 8.11

concepts.statement: Humidity is the measure of water vapour in the air; on rainy, humid days evaporation is slower and clothes dry slowly, and rain is what falls when cloud droplets grow heavy.
concepts.section_ref: 8.2 Another Mystery / 8.5 How can Water be Evaporated Faster or Slower? / 8.7

concepts.statement: Supplying heat turns ice to water and water to vapour while removing heat freezes water, and because evaporation takes heat from the water left behind, a porous earthen matka, a pot-in-pot cooler or water sprinkled on a floor cools things down.
concepts.section_ref: 8.4 How can We Change the States of Water? / 8.6 Cooling Effect / Activity 8.9

concepts.statement: Only a small fraction of Earth's water is available to living things, the rest lying in the oceans, so water must be used wisely and water bodies kept free of pollution; an Atmospheric Water Generator can even harvest water by condensing humid air.
concepts.section_ref: 8.7 closing note / 8.4 'More to Know' (Atmospheric Water Generator)

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
chapters.one_line: Nine everyday separation methods — handpicking, threshing, winnowing, sieving, evaporation, sedimentation and decantation, filtration, churning and magnetic separation — told through a journey across India.

concepts.statement: A dissolved solid such as salt is recovered from water by evaporating the water (in salt pans and by heating a salt solution to dryness), insoluble particles are removed by letting them settle and decanting or by filtering muddy water through filter paper, cloth, cotton, sand or charcoal, and oil is decanted off water because it forms a separate layer.
concepts.section_ref: Evaporation (Activities 9.2, 9.3) / Sedimentation and Decantation / Filtration (Activities 9.4, 9.5)

concepts.statement: Evaporation — a liquid turning into its vapour — is put to work to separate a dissolved solid from water, whether by sunlight and air over seawater in shallow pits or by boiling a salt solution away over a spirit lamp.
concepts.section_ref: Evaporation / Activities 9.2, 9.3

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Living Creatures: Exploring their Characteristics
chapters.one_line: Living beings are distinguished from non-living by movement, growth, nutrition, respiration, excretion, response to stimuli and reproduction; then seed germination and the life cycles of a bean plant, a mosquito and a frog are traced.

concepts.statement: A seed needs water and air (not light) to germinate — water softens the seed coat so the embryo can grow — while mosquitoes lay eggs on stagnant water where larvae and pupae surface to breathe, and frogs begin life as spawn and tadpoles swimming in ponds before living on both land and water.
concepts.section_ref: 10.2 Essential Conditions for Germination of a Seed (Activity 10.2) / 10.5.1 Life cycle of a mosquito (Activity 10.5) / 10.5.2 Life cycle of a frog (Activity 10.6)

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Nature's Treasures
chapters.one_line: Air, water, sunlight, forests, soil, rocks, minerals and fossil fuels are natural resources, classified as renewable or non-renewable and to be used responsibly.

concepts.statement: Water is a precious resource because most of it is saline and only a very small fraction of freshwater is easily accessible, so wastage in hand washing, cooking and gardening should be cut by turning off taps, fixing leaks, recycling water and harvesting rainwater — access is unequal across India, and water counts as a renewable resource only when used judiciously.
concepts.section_ref: 11.2 (water as a natural resource) / Activity 11.3 / 11.7 (renewable resources)

concepts.statement: Water covers about two-thirds of the Earth's surface, but most of it lies in oceans and seas as saline water, with freshwater held in ice sheets and snow, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells and underground sources.
concepts.section_ref: 11.2 (water as a natural resource)

concepts.statement: Rainwater harvesting is an age-old Indian practice, seen in traditional stepwells — the Bawadi of Rajasthan and the Vav of Gujarat — that store rainwater and water seeping from nearby ponds and lakes.
concepts.section_ref: 11.2 (water as a natural resource)

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Oceans and Continents
chapters.one_line: Maps the distribution of water and land on Earth — five interconnected oceans, seven continents and islands — and shows how oceans sustain life, drive rainfall, shape human history and also bring cyclones and tsunamis.

concepts.statement: Water covers almost three-fourths of the Earth, mostly as five named but continuously connected oceans (Pacific the largest, Arctic the smallest) whose seas, bays and gulfs are parts of one global body, the Southern Hemisphere is mostly water, and freshwater is only a small share found in glaciers, rivers, lakes, the atmosphere and underground.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Distribution of Water and Land on the Earth (polar-view map activity) / Section: Oceans

concepts.statement: Oceans drive the water cycle by generating the rainfall that keeps continents from being deserts, which is why clouds forming over the ocean are the source of India's summer monsoon.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Oceans and Life / Section: Oceans and Disasters

concepts.statement: India's summer monsoon rains originate over the ocean, and the same oceans generate cyclones — violent storms with extreme rainfall and strong winds that damage coastal regions.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Oceans and Disasters

concepts.statement: Every layer of the ocean from sunlit surface to dark depths hosts marine flora (algae, seaweeds) and marine fauna (fish, dolphins, whales), the ocean's plant life makes more than half the world's oxygen, and salty seawater is unfit for land animals to drink.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Oceans / Section: Oceans and Life

concepts.statement: From earliest times people have used seas and oceans to migrate, trade, wage military campaigns and fish, coastal cultures built tales and legends around the sea, and ocean-born tsunamis such as the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami are now met with early warning systems and the National Disaster Management Authority.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Oceans and Life / Section: Oceans and Disasters

chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: Landforms and Life
chapters.one_line: Classifies the Earth's surface into mountains, plateaus and plains (plus deserts), describing each landform's environment, the life and livelihoods it supports, and the challenges and cultural meanings people attach to it.

concepts.statement: Snow melting on mountains feeds rivers such as the 2,500 km Ganga with its Himalayan tributaries, rivers plunge off plateau edges as waterfalls (Jog, Hundru, Nohkalikai, Victoria), and rivers rising in mountains carry rock, sand and silt down to deposit them as the fertile soils of floodplains.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Mountains (Don't Miss Out: the Ganga) / Section: Plateaus (waterfalls) / Section: Plains (floodplains)

concepts.statement: Precipitation is defined as water reaching the ground as rain, snow or hail, deserts are the landform that receives very little of it, and cloudbursts, flash floods and heavy snowfall are among the hazards of mountain life.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Mountains (key vocabulary) / Section: Life in the mountains (activity on challenges) / Section: Life in the plains (deserts)

concepts.statement: Farming on the Ganga plain, once rainfed, now depends heavily on irrigation from canals and groundwater, which has raised production but depleted groundwater — a challenge for the future.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Life in the plains

concepts.statement: The first civilisations grew up around rivers in fertile plains, river sources and confluences are held sacred with festivals and rituals in India, rivers carry navigation and trade, and the Sangam tiṇai Neydal ties coastal life to fishing and seafaring.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Life in the plains (river-visit activity; the five tiṇais)

explicit_links: prompting students to connect poetry to geography
chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation
chapters.one_line: Defines what makes a civilisation and traces the Sindhu-Sarasvatī (Harappan) civilisation from river-valley villages to planned cities with drainage, wells and reservoirs, through its crafts, food and trade, to its decline as rainfall fell and the Sarasvatī dried.

concepts.statement: India's first civilisation grew on the plains watered by the Indus and the Sarasvatī, and its planned cities counted water and drainage management as a mark of urbanism — the waterproofed Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro, hundreds of brick-lined wells, and Dholavira's six stone or rock-cut reservoirs (the largest 73 m long) linked by underground drains.
concepts.section_ref: Section: What Is a Civilisation? / Section: From Village to City / Section: Town-Planning (Great Bath debate) / Section: Water Management

concepts.statement: Harappans drew water from brick-lined wells, ponds and streams, and where these were lacking built human-made reservoirs that harvested and distributed water — an infrastructure that needed organised administration to build and maintain.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Water Management (reservoir-measuring activity; Think About It on administration)

concepts.statement: Harappan homes had bathing areas connected to a city-wide drainage network beneath the streets that carried waste water away — an early system of sanitation.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Water Management

concepts.statement: Settlements were placed along rivers both for water and for the fertile soil rivers create, and the Sarasvatī — today the seasonal Ghaggar in India and Hakra in Pakistan — is a river that later texts describe drying up and disappearing.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Sarasvatī River / Section: What Did the Harappans Eat?

concepts.statement: A global climatic change from about 2200 BCE reduced rainfall and made farming harder, which together with the drying of the Sarasvatī in its central basin led to the abandonment of cities such as Kalibangan and Banawali.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The End or a New Beginning?

chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: The Day the River Spoke (Learning Together)
chapters.one_line: In Kamala Nair's story a personified River counsels Jahnavi, a coastal-village girl kept home from school, to slip into class and claim her right to learn.

concepts.statement: The River is a living character who listens to a village girl and counsels her to go to school, and children go on to discuss why India's rivers are held sacred and mostly addressed as female (the Brahmaputra and Sone being male) and to name the country's boats — canoe, catamaran, coracle, shikara — and other water-transport words (boats placed here as the nearest fit in the vocabulary).
concepts.section_ref: Section A: The Day the River Spoke (prose_summary) / Let us think and reflect I Extract 1 / Let us learn I, IV, V / Let us explore I

chapters.subject: english

chapters.title: The World of Metals and Non-metals
chapters.one_line: Metals and non-metals are distinguished by malleability, ductility, sonority and conduction, then by how they behave with air and water — rusting, basic metal oxides, acidic non-metal oxides.

concepts.statement: Iron rusts only when both water and air are present (a nail in boiled, oil-covered water or in dry air stays clean), sodium is stored in kerosene to keep it from water while phosphorus is stored under water, and sulfur dioxide dissolves in water to give an acidic solution — water here is a reactant and storage medium, which has no id of its own, so it is placed under the nearest (water-as-solvent).
concepts.section_ref: 4.2 Effect of Air and Water on Metals: Iron / 4.3 Effect of Air and Water on Other Metals / 4.4 Substances that Behave Differently from Metals in Air and Water

explicit_links: build a tester circuit (as in Chapter 3)
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical
chapters.one_line: Changes are sorted into physical and chemical, reversible and irreversible, desirable and undesirable, ending with the slow natural changes of weathering and erosion.

concepts.statement: Ice melting, water boiling or evaporating and wet clothes drying are physical changes — the water stays water in all three states — and they are reversible, since melted ice can be refrozen and evaporated water condensed, unlike burning wood or making popcorn.
concepts.section_ref: 5.1 A Substance May Change in Appearance but Remain the Same! / Activity 5.1 / 5.5 Are Changes Permanent? (Activity 5.8)

concepts.statement: Rocks break into sediments by weathering — water freezing in cracks, temperature swings, growing roots, and water with dissolved chemicals reacting with rock surfaces — and flowing water and wind then carry the sediments away (erosion) to settle in water bodies where, over thousands of years, they harden into new rock.
concepts.section_ref: 5.7.1 Weathering of rocks / 5.7.2 Erosion

explicit_links: Rusting revisits the formation of rust from Chapter 4
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Heat Transfer in Nature
chapters.one_line: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation, and these modes explain land and sea breezes, the water cycle and the seepage of rainwater into the ground.

concepts.statement: Water heats by convection — warmed water at the base expands, rises and is replaced by cooler water, as a potassium permanganate trace shows — and because land heats and cools faster than water, air flows from sea to land by day (sea breeze) and from land to sea at night (land breeze), while a pan of water on a flame uses conduction, convection and radiation at once.
concepts.section_ref: 7.2 Convection / 7.2.1 Land and Sea Breeze (Activity 7.4) / 7.3 Radiation

concepts.statement: Solar radiation drives evaporation from oceans, rivers and lakes and transpiration from plants, the rising vapour cools and condenses into clouds, and precipitation as rain, snow or hail returns water through soil, rocks and plants to the water bodies — with water present in nature as liquid, as snow, ice sheets and glaciers, and as vapour.
concepts.section_ref: 7.4 Water Cycle

concepts.statement: Rain seeps into the ground fastest through gravel and slowest through clay (infiltration) to become groundwater held in aquifers that wells and bore wells tap, and since over-extraction and urban concrete are depleting it, rainwater harvesting and recharge pits are needed — Ladakh's ice stupas store winter stream water as ice to release for farming in summer.
concepts.section_ref: 7.4.1 Seepage of water beneath the Earth / Science and Society box (ice stupa)

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Nutrition and Respiration in Animals (summary carries no chapter title; named from its sections 9.1 and 9.2)
chapters.one_line: Animals digest food along the alimentary canal and respire to release energy from it, with variations such as rumination, gizzards, gills and skin breathing.

concepts.statement: The large intestine absorbs water from undigested food, respiration in cells releases water along with carbon dioxide and energy, and fish breathe by passing dissolved oxygen from the surrounding water into the blood through gills, while tadpoles use gills and frogs and earthworms exchange gases through moist skin.
concepts.section_ref: 9.1.1 Large intestine / 9.2.1 How does the exchange of gases happen? / 9.2.2 Do other animals breathe the same way as humans do?

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Life Processes in Plants
chapters.one_line: Plants make food by photosynthesis from carbon dioxide and water in sunlight with chlorophyll, transport water through xylem and food through phloem, and respire like animals.

concepts.statement: Plants need water to grow (a sapling in sunlight without water fails), water is a raw material of photosynthesis (carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen), and roots absorb water with dissolved minerals that travel upward through xylem tubes, as a stem cutting in red-inked water shows.
concepts.section_ref: 10.1 How Do Plants Grow? (Activity 10.1) / 10.2.3 Photosynthesis: in a nutshell / 10.3.1 Transport of water and minerals (Activity 10.7)

explicit_links: connects to Grade 6 learning that all living beings need food for growth, and to Chapter 9's discussion of how animals obtain nutrition
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Geographical Diversity of India
chapters.one_line: Tours India's physical regions — Himalayas, Ladakh, Gangetic plains, Thar, Aravallis, peninsular plateau, coasts, islands, the Sundarbans and the Northeast hills — and the life, resources and culture each supports.

concepts.statement: Summer snow-melt from the Himalayas — the Bhagirathi rising at Gaumukh from the Gangotri Glacier — feeds the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra whose mineral-laden waters build the fertile Gangetic plains, the eastward tilt of the peninsular plateau sends the Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Mahanadi to the Bay of Bengal as wide fertile deltas while the Narmada and Tapti flow west into estuaries, and the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta forms the mangrove Sundarbans.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Himalayas as a Water Tower / Section: The Gangetic Plains / Section: The Peninsular Plateau / Section: India's Amazing Coastlines / Section: The Delta in West Bengal and the Sundarbans

concepts.statement: The Himalayas are the 'Water Tower of Asia' whose rivers supply drinking, farming and industrial water to hundreds of millions, while in the water-scarce Thar people conserve rain with traditional taanka or kund rainwater-harvesting systems.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Himalayas as a Water Tower / Section: The Great Indian Desert — Thar Desert

concepts.statement: The Arabian Sea, Indian Ocean and Bay of Bengal bound the subcontinent and hold its two island groups, and India's inland water bodies range from Ladakh's saltwater Pangong Tso to the east-coast Chilika Lake and Pulicat lagoon.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Introduction: India as a Subcontinent / Section: The Cold Desert of India — Ladakh / Section: India's Amazing Coastlines / Section: Indian Islands

concepts.statement: Rainfall varies from extremely scarce in the cold desert of Ladakh to among the highest in the world in the Garo, Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Cold Desert of India — Ladakh / Section: The Hills of the Northeast

chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: Understanding the Weather
chapters.one_line: Defines weather and its five elements — temperature, precipitation, pressure, wind and humidity — explains how each is measured, and shows how weather stations and the IMD turn those readings into forecasts and warnings.

concepts.statement: Precipitation (rain, snow, sleet or hail) is measured with a rain gauge whose scale reads rainfall in millimetres, humidity — the water vapour in the air — is measured by a hygrometer as relative humidity from dry (20–40%) to humid (60–80%), and these readings, alongside traditional signs such as ants moving eggs or frogs croaking, feed forecasts of rain, of the monsoon's arrival and IMD colour-coded heavy-rain warnings.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Weather and its Elements / Section: Weather Instruments b) Precipitation / e) Humidity / Section: Predicting the Weather

concepts.statement: The IMD's motto 'From the sun arises rain', taken from the Manusmṛiti's 'from the sun arises rain, from rain comes food, and from food, living beings originate', is presented as the ancient understanding of the sun's role in the water cycle.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Weather Instruments a) Temperature (IMD motto)

chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: Climates of India
chapters.one_line: Distinguishes weather, seasons and climate, surveys India's climate types and the factors behind them, explains the monsoon's mechanism and its hold on culture and economy, and covers climate-linked disasters and climate change.

concepts.statement: The monsoon is a seasonal wind reversal — in summer the heated Asian landmass forms a low that draws moisture-laden ocean winds inland to drop heavy rain (the south-west monsoon advancing from early June to cover India by mid-July, the Western Ghats leaving the Deccan in a rain shadow, Mawsynram receiving about 11,000 mm a year), while in winter dry winds blow from land to sea except where the north-east monsoon gathers Bay of Bengal moisture for the east and south — and a failed monsoon means scarcity, higher food prices and migration.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Monsoons / Section: Factors Determining the Climate — Winds, Topography / Section: Types of Climates in India / Section: Climate and our Lives

concepts.statement: Because the sea absorbs and releases heat more slowly than land, coastal Mumbai has a yearly temperature range of about 14°C against inland Nagpur's 34°C, and this same land–ocean heating difference creates the pressure contrasts that drive the monsoon winds.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Factors Determining the Climate — Proximity to the Sea / Section: The Monsoons

concepts.statement: Cooler, moisture-laden winds drawn in from the ocean condense their moisture over the heated land and drop it as heavy monsoon rain, and winds crossing the Bay of Bengal collect moisture again for east and south India — the ocean-to-rain leg of the water cycle.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Factors Determining the Climate — Winds / Section: The Monsoons

concepts.statement: Floods occur when heavy rain, river-bank breaches or bursting glacial lakes send water over normally dry land — as in the 2013 Kedarnath disaster — and urban flooding is worsened by poor drainage, encroached waterways and impermeable concrete.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Climates and Disasters — Floods

concepts.statement: The arid Thar demands unique water conservation practices, and a failed monsoon brings water scarcity that hurts farming and the industries that depend on predictable water availability.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Types of Climates in India / Section: Climate and our Lives

chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
chapters.one_line: Cells, levels of organisation and microorganisms are introduced through the microscope, with microbes' roles in decomposition, food and water.
explicit_links: inside the human gut (helping with digestion, as introduced in Grade 7)
sub-cellular components that will be studied in higher classes
chapters.skip_reason: Water appears only as a sampling medium (pond or stagnant water observed under the microscope, a water-filled flask used as a lens) and as the habitat of microalgae; the chapter teaches cells and microorganisms, not any water concept.
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Pressure, Winds, Storms, and Cyclones
chapters.one_line: Pressure — in solids, liquids and the atmosphere — explains winds, sea and land breezes, storms, lightning and cyclones.

concepts.statement: Overhead water tanks are placed high to supply good pressure and dam bases are built broader than their tops to withstand the large sideways water pressure near the bottom, because liquid pressure depends on the height of the water column and acts in all directions (liquid pressure itself has no id; placed under the nearest).
concepts.section_ref: 6.1 Pressure (Activities 6.1, 6.2; 'Ever heard of…' on dams)

concepts.statement: Sea and land breezes are re-explained through pressure: by day the faster-heating land warms the air above it into a low-pressure area that cooler sea air flows into, and at night the warmer sea reverses the flow.
concepts.section_ref: 6.3 Formation of Wind

concepts.statement: Storms form when warm moist air rises, expands and cools so its water vapour condenses into clouds and the droplets merge to fall as rain, hail or snow; ice particles and droplets rubbing inside the cloud build the charges that discharge as lightning in a thunderstorm (Kalboishakhi, Bordoisila and mango showers are pre-monsoon examples), and cyclones bring intense winds and heavy rainfall around a calm eye.
concepts.section_ref: 6.5 Storms, Thunderstorms, and Lightning / 6.6 Cyclone

concepts.statement: A cyclone is powered by warm ocean water — rising moist air condenses and releases latent heat that deepens the low pressure — weakens once it reaches land and loses its moist air, and drives storm surges of 3–12 metres that flood coasts and contaminate drinking water with seawater.
concepts.section_ref: 6.6 Cyclone

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Particulate Nature of Matter
chapters.one_line: All matter is made of tiny constituent particles whose spacing, attraction and motion explain the solid, liquid and gaseous states and the changes between them.

concepts.statement: Ice, water and vapour are explained by particles: in ice they only vibrate in fixed positions, at the melting point (0 °C) they break free to move within a limited space, at the boiling point they escape as vapour with bubbles forming throughout the bulk, whereas evaporation happens only at the surface at any temperature — and water, unlike air, is practically incompressible.
concepts.section_ref: 7.2.1 Solid state / 7.2.2 Liquid state (Activity 7.4) / 7.3 (Activity 7.6)

concepts.statement: Sugar dissolved in water turns invisible but is still there (its taste proves it) because its particles slip into the spaces between water particles, so the solution's volume is less than the sum of the two, whereas insoluble sand settles and adds volume; a grain of potassium permanganate spreading through water — faster in hot water — shows that water particles are always moving.
concepts.section_ref: 7.1 (Activity 7.2) / 7.3 (Activity 7.7) / 7.4 (Activity 7.8, 'Think Like a Scientist')

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
chapters.one_line: Matter is classified into mixtures and pure substances — elements and compounds — with minerals as naturally occurring elements and compounds.

concepts.statement: Sugar dissolved in water is the model uniform mixture (components indistinguishable even under a microscope), sand-in-water and seawater are solid–liquid mixtures and oxygen-in-water a gas–liquid one, while water itself is shown by passing electricity through it to be a compound of hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed 2:1 ratio — a fact about water's own make-up with no id of its own, placed here as nearest.
concepts.section_ref: 8.1 What Are Mixtures? / 8.1.2 Types of mixtures (Table 8.1) / 8.3 What Are the Types of Pure Substances? (Activity 8.3) / 8.3.2 Compounds

explicit_links: revisits the composition of air, confirmed from earlier learning
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
chapters.one_line: Solutions are defined through solute, solvent, saturation, concentration and solubility (of solids and gases with temperature); then density and its measurement explain floating and sinking.

concepts.statement: In a salt–water solution the dissolved solid is the solute and water the solvent; a fixed volume of water dissolves only so much salt before the solution is saturated, solubility of most solids rises with temperature (baking soda at 20, 50 and 70 °C) while that of gases falls, and concentration separates dilute from concentrated solutions.
concepts.section_ref: 9.1 What Are Solute, Solvent, and Solution? / 9.2 (Activity 9.1) / 9.2.1 (Activity 9.2) / 9.3 Solubility of Gases

concepts.statement: Colder water holds more dissolved oxygen, so warming water leaves fish short of oxygen, and because ice is less dense than water it floats and insulates the water beneath, keeping aquatic life alive in cold climates.
concepts.section_ref: 9.3 Solubility of Gases / 9.5.2 Effect of temperature on density

concepts.statement: Water volume is read on a measuring cylinder (5 mL to 500 mL sizes) at its least count with the eye level to the meniscus — Activity 9.5 measures out exactly 50 mL — and the rise in water level when an irregular object is submerged gives that object's volume, while a digital balance with tare gives mass in grams.
concepts.section_ref: 9.5.1 Determination of density (Activities 9.3, 9.4, 9.5, 9.7)

concepts.statement: Water is densest at 4 °C and expands as it freezes into ice at 0 °C, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats — the anomalous behaviour of water.
concepts.section_ref: 9.5.2 Effect of temperature on density

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
chapters.one_line: Earth's position, size, atmosphere and magnetic field keep water liquid and life possible, sustained by the interplay of hydrosphere, geosphere, biosphere and atmosphere and now threatened by the triple planetary crisis.

concepts.statement: Earth sits in the habitable (Goldilocks) zone where temperatures keep water liquid — closer to the Sun it would evaporate, farther away it would freeze — and the atmosphere's mild greenhouse effect is what holds that liquid range.
concepts.section_ref: 13.3.1 Position of the Earth / 13.2 What Do the Planets of Our Solar System Look Like?

concepts.statement: Water covering about 70 per cent of Earth's surface — ponds, rivers, seas, oceans and groundwater — forms the hydrosphere, which is why Earth looks like the Blue Planet from space, and melting ice caps now raise sea levels that flood coastal areas.
concepts.section_ref: 13.4.1 Air, water, and sunlight / 13.3.1 Position of the Earth / 13.6 What Are the Threats to Life on Earth?

concepts.statement: Liquid water is essential for life to evolve and be sustained: it acts as a solvent, transports nutrients in plants, regulates body temperature in animals, aids digestion and supports aquatic life from plankton to whales, while water pollution from industrial, agricultural and plastic waste harms that life.
concepts.section_ref: 13.4.1 Air, water, and sunlight / 13.6 What Are the Threats to Life on Earth?

concepts.statement: Water vapour forms clouds that bring rain and snow, refilling rivers and lakes and deciding which plants and animals can live in a region — and cutting down a forest can change the rainfall.
concepts.section_ref: 13.4.1 Air, water, and sunlight / 13.4.4 The importance of balance

explicit_links: revisits the solar system from prior learning
echoing content from Chapter 12 on ecology
the concluding chapter of the middle-stage science journey
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Natural Resources and Their Use
chapters.one_line: Explains when Nature becomes a resource, categorises resources by use and renewability, shows how uneven distribution shapes settlement and conflict, and argues for stewardship through cases of groundwater over-extraction, cement and organic farming.

concepts.statement: Water is a renewable resource only while Nature's rhythm of restoration is not disturbed: farmers across India pump groundwater for irrigation faster than it recharges so water tables fall, Punjab's Green Revolution crops and free electricity have left almost 80 per cent of its area 'overexploited' with groundwater beyond about 30 metres, Himalayan glaciers melt faster than precipitation replaces them, and the remedies are water harvesting, pond rejuvenation and reduced consumption.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Resources essential for life / Section: Renewable resources / Section: Restoration and regeneration of renewable resources / Section: Overexploitation of groundwater: a caselet from Punjab

concepts.statement: Water resources that cross political boundaries generate inter-state and international tensions, as with the Kaveri River shared among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications

concepts.statement: Water, with air and food, is a resource life cannot exist without and humans cannot manufacture, yet chemical contamination of over-pumped groundwater in Punjab and cement-industry pollution now pose health hazards, and access to water is inequitably distributed with the poor bearing the burden.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Resources essential for life / Section: Overexploitation of groundwater: a caselet from Punjab / Section: The case of cement / Section: The International Solar Alliance (closing paragraph)

chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: World Geography: Some Glimpses
chapters.one_line: A guided tour of the Earth's physical features — from map projections to the oceans, currents, trenches and reefs, then continent by continent through plateaus, deserts, steppes, mountains, plains and rivers — and the human activities and environmental pressures tied to each.

concepts.statement: The ocean covers about 71 per cent of the Earth and holds 97 per cent of its water over a floor of mountains, valleys and trenches (the Mariana's Challenger Deep over 11,000 m down); the five oceans are revisited with their distinct features, ocean currents run like giant rivers carrying warm water poleward and cold water toward the equator, seas, gulfs, bays, straits and canals are classified by shape and trade role, and the Great Lakes are a chain of five massive freshwater lakes.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Blue of the Blue Planet, the Oceans / Section: The oceans / Section: Ocean currents / Section: Ocean trenches / Section: Smaller water bodies and waterways / Section: North America (The Great Lakes)

concepts.statement: Oceans regulate climate by absorbing heat and releasing it slowly, and warm currents such as the Gulf Stream carry equatorial heat north through the Atlantic so that the United Kingdom is warmer than other places at the same latitude.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Blue of the Blue Planet, the Oceans / Section: Ocean currents

concepts.statement: Oceans add moisture to the air that forms clouds and rainfall, which is how the distant Southern Indian Ocean influences the monsoon in the Gangetic Plains.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Introduction / Section: The Blue of the Blue Planet, the Oceans

concepts.statement: Oceans support life from plankton to the blue whale and supply almost half the oxygen we breathe, trench organisms live in total darkness on chemical energy instead of photosynthesis, and coral reefs — 'rainforests of the sea' sheltering a quarter of all ocean species — are bleaching as human actions change ocean chemistry.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Blue of the Blue Planet, the Oceans (plankton activity) / Section: Ocean trenches / Section: The Great Barrier Reef

concepts.statement: Mountains act as 'water towers' — the Tibetan 'Third Pole' sources the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze and its snow-melt is now expanding lakes, the Alps feed the Rhine and Danube, the Andes feed the Amazon (the largest river by volume) — while plains such as the European Plain are built by sediment deposition and the Colorado Plateau's Grand Canyon is cut by erosion.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Asia (Roof of the world; The Urals) / Section: Europe (The European Plain; the Alps) / Section: South America / Section: North America (Colorado Plateau)

concepts.statement: Rivers, mountains and lakes are freshwater suppliers — the Nile's irrigation, drinking water and hydropower, the Alps' drinking water, irrigation and hydroelectricity, the Andes as a source for millions, the Great Lakes' city water now facing chemical contamination — while desert life clusters at Sahara oases and Gobi pastures fed by underground water.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Africa (the Nile; the Sahara) / Section: Europe (the Alps) / Section: South America (the Andes) / Section: North America (The Great Lakes) / Section: Asia (Gobi Desert)

concepts.statement: River valleys nurtured some of the world's earliest civilisations — the Nile was the cradle of ancient Egypt — and waterways carry trade: the Persian Gulf linked India and Europe for millennia, bays shelter ports and dockyards, and the Suez Canal (1869) made the shortest sea route from India to Europe.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Europe (The European Plain) / Section: Africa (the Nile) / Section: Smaller water bodies and waterways

Building on Grade 6, this section revisits the five oceans
recalling from Grade 6 the definitions of mountains, plateaus, and plains
Because Part 1 of the textbook covered India's major landforms, the tour deliberately focuses on other parts of the world
chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: A Journey Through Indian Architecture
chapters.one_line: A guided journey through representative Indian structures — Harappan cities, stupas, rock-cut caves, water structures, temples, mosques, forts and palaces, tombs, traditional houses, churches and colonial buildings — and the thought behind them.

concepts.statement: Water structures are a distinct strand of Indian architecture: from Harappan drainage, Dholavira's reservoirs and interlocking trapezoid-brick wells, through Shringaverpur's Ganga-fed chain of reservoirs with silt-settling tanks, to the stepwells (vāvs, bāorīs such as Rani ki Vav) of Gujarat and Rajasthan that stored rainwater and gave a cool social space, temple tanks (puṣhkariṇīs) for harvesting and ritual, the Grand Anicut, and Agra Fort's Persian wheels lifting Yamuna water to fountains that cooled the palace.
concepts.section_ref: Section: The Beginnings … / Section: Water Structures / Section: Forts and Palaces (Red Fort at Agra box)

concepts.statement: Because India's monsoon delivers water seasonally, people over millennia built structures to harvest, store and distribute it — from the village pond to the Grand Anicut — suited to each region's geology and climate, and many now suffer from depleted sources, poor maintenance, pollution and waste dumping that environmentalists, locals and NGOs work to reverse.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Water Structures

a "Let's Remember" box on where these caves appear in earlier textbooks
Forts are recalled from earlier chapters
a "Let's Remember" box asks students to recall the forts of Jaisalmer, Kumbhalgarh, Raigad and Sindhudurg and locate them on the map
chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: India's Urban Landscape
chapters.one_line: Examines what makes a place urban, how cities become economic and cultural hubs, the strains of rapid urbanisation — water, sanitation, slums, pollution — and how planning, from Jaipur to Singapore and Bengaluru's lake revival, can answer them.

concepts.statement: Cities have always depended on water — places near rivers grew into trade centres, Harappan Dholavira had complex water structures, and Jaipur was laid out in 1727 with reservoirs and canals for a steady supply in a dry climate — and today water supply and sewerage are core problems of urban planning, eased in Delhi by spreading growth across the National Capital Region and built into Singapore's master plans and Ahmedabad's Sabarmati Riverfront.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Introduction / Section: How do Cities Become Centres of Economic Activities? / Section: What Leads to Urbanisation? (Delhi) / Section: Planning Our Cities / Section: India's 'Pink City' (Panna Meena Kund stepwell)

concepts.statement: Bengaluru suffers summer water shortages and monsoon flooding because of poor planning, groundwater overuse, no rainwater harvesting and encroached lake beds — its roughly 1,000 lakes reduced to about 200 — and non-profits, resident associations and communities have revived lakes such as Yelahanka by desilting, repairing bunds, clearing drainage channels and replanting, increasing water availability.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Challenges Faced by Cities / Section: Power of collective action in the revival of Bengaluru lakes

concepts.statement: Unplanned urban growth and slums leave residents with poor access to water and sanitation, while sewage- and chemical-polluted lakes such as Bellandur and Varthur foam, release toxic gases and even catch fire.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Challenges Faced by Cities / Section: Power of collective action in the revival of Bengaluru lakes

chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: Cell: The Building Block of Life
chapters.one_line: Cells are studied through the microscope, their membrane and wall, their organelles, cell division by mitosis and meiosis, and the Cell Theory.

concepts.statement: Water moves into and out of cells by osmosis — diffusion across the selectively permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated solution — so a potato piece or cheek cell shrinks in 20% salt or sugar solution and a plant cell plasmolyses while its wall holds its outer shape, and the water-filled central vacuole's turgor keeps plant cells firm until water deficit makes the plant wilt.
concepts.section_ref: 2.2.1 Cell membrane (Activity 2.2, What if…) / 2.2.2 Cell wall (Activity 2.3) / 2.3.1 Vacuoles

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Tissues in Action
chapters.one_line: Plant meristematic and permanent tissues and the four animal tissue types are described, ending with joints and the musculoskeletal system.

concepts.statement: Water enters through root hairs that enlarge the root's absorbing surface, rises through xylem's dead tracheids and vessels, and leaves through stomata as transpiration — a loss the waxy cuticle limits (thicker in dry habitats) but which also creates the transpiration pull that keeps water moving upward against gravity.
concepts.section_ref: 3.2.4 (i) Protective tissue — Epidermis / (iii) Conducting tissues — Complex permanent tissues / Pause and Ponder 2–4

explicit_links: connecting to the mitosis observed in onion root tips in Chapter 2
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Exploring Mixtures and their Separation
chapters.one_line: Mixtures are classified as homogeneous or heterogeneous and separated by crystallization, distillation, chromatography, separating funnel, sublimation, centrifugation and coagulation, with solutions, suspensions and colloids told apart by the Tyndall effect.

concepts.statement: Water solutions are now quantified — concentration as % m/m, % m/v or % v/v (ORS and 0.9% saline must be exact) and solubility read from curves against temperature — and separated by crystallizing a cooled saturated solution (copper sulfate; salt from seawater brine), distilling off a lower-boiling liquid such as acetone or recovering the solvent, running ink up chromatography paper with water as the solvent, draining oil from water in a separating funnel, and clearing suspended particles by filtration, centrifugation or alum coagulation, while colloids such as milk scatter light.
concepts.section_ref: 5.2 Solutions (5.2.1–5.2.3, Activity 5.2) / 5.3 Methods of Separation of Homogeneous Mixtures (Activities 5.3, 5.4, 5.5) / 5.4 (Activities 5.6, 5.8; 5.4.3 Suspensions; 5.4.4 Colloids) / 5.5 Tyndall Effect

concepts.statement: Distillation exploits water's 100 °C boiling point — a lower-boiling liquid like acetone (56 °C) is boiled off first and condensed in a water-cooled condenser — and clouds of water droplets or ice crystals in air are posed as a colloid puzzle, with snowflakes and frost cited as natural crystals.
concepts.section_ref: 5.3.2 Distillation / 5.3.1 Crystallization / 5.4.4 Colloids (Pause and Ponder)

chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Atomic Foundations of Matter
chapters.one_line: The laws of conservation of mass and constant proportions lead to Dalton's atomic theory, covalent and ionic bonding, formula writing and molecular and formula unit masses.

concepts.statement: Ionic compounds such as salt and copper sulfate dissolve in water (not in kerosene or petrol) and their solutions conduct electricity because the ions become free to move, sugar dissolves without conducting, and camphor and naphthalene do not dissolve at all — while water itself is treated as a compound (hydrogen and oxygen always 1:8 by mass whatever the source, two single covalent bonds in H₂O, molecular mass 18 u), a fact with no id of its own placed here as nearest.
concepts.section_ref: 9.6 Properties of the Ionic and the Covalent Compounds (Activity 9.4) / 9.1 (Activity 9.1) / 9.2 Law of Constant Proportions / 9.4.1 B Molecules of compounds / 9.7

explicit_links: The section recalls from Chapter 8 that atoms with eight electrons in the valence shell (or two electrons if the K-shell is outermost) are stable
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Reproduction: How Life Continues
chapters.one_line: Asexual and sexual reproduction in plants, animals and humans, from vegetative propagation and meiosis to pollination, fertilisation, pregnancy and reproductive health.
chapters.skip_reason: Water appears only incidentally — as the medium of external fertilisation in fish and frogs, one pollination agent among four, and a seed-dispersal and germination condition; the chapter teaches reproduction, not a water concept.
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
chapters.one_line: Biodiversity is organised through the five-kingdom system, plant and animal groups, hierarchical ranks, binomial naming and fossil evidence.

concepts.statement: The plant kingdom is ordered by its dependence on water: thallophytes are aquatic, bryophytes and pteridophytes live on land but still need water for their swimming male gametes, and gymnosperms are the first to reproduce without water — while sponges feed on water flowing through their pores and fins and gills fit fish for aquatic life.
concepts.section_ref: 12.6.4 Kingdom Plantae (Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms) / 12.6.5 Porifera / 12.7 Adaptations as Outcomes of Structural Change

explicit_links: compare a cross section of a fern stem (showing its vascular bundles) with the cross section of a sunflower stem studied in Chapter 3
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
chapters.one_line: Earth is one system of five spheres — geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere, biosphere — linked by uneven solar heating, winds and ocean currents, biogeochemical cycles and human impact.

concepts.statement: The water cycle now includes surface runoff back to the ocean and infiltration into soil and rock, where water dissolves and carries minerals, and it links all five spheres — so a warmer atmosphere holding more moisture brings heavier rains in some places and droughts in others, while intense rainfall erodes soil and cuts groundwater recharge.
concepts.section_ref: 13.3.1 Water cycle / Activity 13.1

concepts.statement: Surface water and groundwater form the hydrosphere and ice and snow the cryosphere; ocean currents driven by planetary winds, temperature and salinity differences, Earth's rotation and the continents form gyres that carry heat poleward (the North Atlantic Drift keeps European ports ice-free) and nutrients to marine life, and the ocean holds 71% of global carbon, acidifying as it warms.
concepts.section_ref: Introduction (five spheres) / 13.2.3 Ocean currents / 13.3.2 Carbon cycle / 13.4

concepts.statement: Nearly all weather happens in the troposphere, and the monsoon is now treated as climate-sensitive: warmer Arabian Sea water intensifies the southwest monsoon, deforestation lowers local rainfall, and IITM Pune's coupled atmosphere–ocean–land–ice models forecast how warming may alter monsoon rainfall.
concepts.section_ref: Introduction / 13.1.3 Role of the atmosphere / 13.4 Human Impact on Earth's Processes / IITM feature

concepts.statement: Water shapes Earth's heat budget: water vapour is a greenhouse gas, dark ocean water (low albedo) absorbs heat while snow and ice reflect it, and ocean currents move heat from the equator toward the poles, regulating climate.
concepts.section_ref: 13.1 Uneven Heating of the Earth / 13.1.1 (Activity 13.2) / 13.2.3 Ocean currents

concepts.statement: Melting glaciers add water to rivers and raise sea levels that threaten coastal cities such as Mumbai and Chennai, and intense rainfall runoff erodes soil.
concepts.section_ref: 13.3.1 Water cycle / 13.3.2 Carbon cycle

concepts.statement: Excess nitrate fertiliser washed into rivers and lakes triggers algal blooms that deplete oxygen and kill fish (eutrophication), and warmer, more acidic seawater threatens plankton and coral reefs.
concepts.section_ref: 13.4 Human Impact on Earth's Processes

explicit_links: integrates ideas about energy flow, atmospheric processes, biogeochemical cycles, and human impact that students explored separately in earlier grades
chapters.subject: science

chapters.title: Shaping of the Earth's Surface
chapters.one_line: Explains how internal forces (plate tectonics) build the Earth's surface and how external agents — running water, glaciers, waves, wind and groundwater — weather, erode and deposit to level it, ending with landform-linked disasters.

concepts.statement: A river shapes land differently along its course — V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids where hard rock resists in the upper course, meanders and oxbow lakes from outer-bank erosion and inner-bank deposition in the middle, deltas, levees and alluvial fans where it meets the sea — while glaciers carve U-shaped valleys, cirques and fjords, leave moraines that dam lakes, and can unleash Glacial Lake Outburst Floods when their ice or moraine dams fail.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Running Water / Section: Waterfall / Section: Meander / Section: Deltas / Section: Glaciers (Chamoli 2021 activity) / Section: GLOFs

concepts.statement: Sea waves and currents are agents of gradation that undercut headlands into cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks and deposit beaches and sand bars that shield settlements from coastal erosion.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Waves and Currents

concepts.statement: Chemical weathering changes minerals by reaction with water and acids, and groundwater dissolving limestone creates karst — caves, stalactites, stalagmites, sinkholes and underground rivers.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Weathering / Section: Agents of Gradation / Section: Underground Water

concepts.statement: Rivers, glaciers and groundwater are used as well as feared: the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) in Tamil Nadu shows rivers harnessed for irrigation, moraine-dammed lakes give water supply, irrigation and hydropower, karst provides fresh water, the Sindhu-Sarasvatī people used contouring, bunding, terracing, dams and canals, and Nagaland's Zabo system of earthen bunds and check dams conserves soil and water and recharges groundwater.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Erosion (Don't Miss Out) / Section: Meander / Section: Glaciers / Section: Underground Water

concepts.statement: The river plains of the Ganga, Nile, Brahmaputra and Indus gave rise to agricultural societies and early cities, coasts and harbours supported trade and cultural contact, ancient water management is documented in the Vedas, Kṛiṣhiparāśhara and Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra, and waterfalls and karst caves carry cultural or religious significance.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Agents of Gradation (Don't Miss Out) / Section: Erosion (Don't Miss Out) / Section: Waterfall / Section: Underground Water

concepts.statement: Heavy continuous rainfall adds weight and reduces friction on slopes to trigger landslides and fills glacial lakes before outbursts, while prolonged drought and low rainfall leave loose dry soil for dust storms.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Landslides / Section: GLOFs / Section: Dust Storms

chapters.subject: social_sciences

chapters.title: Atmosphere and Climate
chapters.one_line: Describes the atmosphere's composition and layers, separates weather from climate and sets out their elements, explains India's seasons and the monsoon's reversal, and closes with climate change and a case study of the 2025 Punjab floods.

concepts.statement: Precipitation falls when saturated air condenses, shaped by prevailing winds, mountains and seasons; India's tropical monsoon climate has four IMD seasons, and the monsoon is a wind reversal — the south-west monsoon (June–September), drawn in by a low over the fast-heating landmass, brings most of India's rain, while the north-east monsoon (October–February) blows seaward and rains mainly on the south-east coast after crossing the Bay of Bengal — mapped by normal dates of advance and retreat, vital to farming, water supply and festivals, and studied by the National Monsoon Mission.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Elements of Weather and Climate / Section: Seasons in India (Table 3.2) / Section: Monsoon (Fig. 3.10, Fig. 3.11)

concepts.statement: Land heats and cools faster than the sea, so by day a sea breeze blows from sea to land and at night a land breeze from land to sea, moderating coastal climates, and the same contrast on a seasonal scale drives the monsoon's reversal.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Elements of Weather and Climate (Fig. 3.8 local winds) / Section: Monsoon

concepts.statement: Water vapour makes up only about 0.1 to 0.4 per cent of the atmosphere yet drives cloud formation, warmer air holds more of it, and precipitation is that vapour condensing out of saturated air as drizzle, rain, snow, sleet or hail.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Composition of the Atmosphere (Fig. 3.2) / Section: Elements of Weather and Climate

concepts.statement: Most water vapour and clouds sit in the troposphere, and the monsoon winds carry moisture gathered over the Indian Ocean, Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal onto the land as rain.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Structure of the Atmosphere / Section: Monsoon

concepts.statement: The 2025 Punjab floods came from heavy monsoon rain swelling the Satluj, Beas, Ravi and Ghaggar in succession, made worse by weak old embankments (dhūsī bāndh), building too close to rivers, silt reducing river and dam capacity and late warnings — and climate change is making floods, droughts, glacier melt and sea-level rise more frequent.
concepts.section_ref: Section: Punjab Floods 2025: A Case Study / Section: Climate Change
